Meeting header:

Auto-summary (auto-generated, may be incomplete):
Quick Optimize walkthrough focused on mapping caching + batching opportunities to Riverbend's user journeys. Discussed tradeoffs: latency vs cost, prefetching vs session affinity, model routing options for tail latency. Agreed next steps: send cost model + run sandbox sim.

Transcript body:
[00:00] Sophie Lane: hey everyone thanks for joining, we'll keep this to about 45, 50 minutes, quick intro then demo of the Optimize lane and a walk through of how batching and KV prefetch could map to your workloads.
[00:12] Daniel Ortiz: thanks Sophie, appreciate it. we, um, we've got Priya and Evan here, we're specifically looking at lowering token spend across our customer support assistant and a summary pipeline. latency is important for live chat but costs for nightly summarization are big.
[00:28] Marcus Chen: great, that's exactly the tradeoffs we'll show — there's different knobs for realtime vs batch. quick question, do you have an existing sessionization pattern or affinity? like are you keeping session state on the client or server?
[00:38] Priya Kumar: server side, we store partial context in Redis currently and we do some short-term KV for the active conversation, it's not persisted beyond a few hours. the summary pipeline is totally separate, it's batched nightly with big payloads.
[00:50] Ibrahim Patel: thanks, that helps. one of the things we'll do today is an 'opportunity map' — where the Console Optimize recommendations give you predicted token-savings and latency delta if you enable prefix prefetch vs session KV vs conservative batching.
[01:05] Lina Park: that sounds super useful yes please.
[01:09] [01:15] Marcus Chen: okay jumping into the console — (screen share) — so on the left is Optimize, you'll see a Cost Savings view and a Playbooks tab. i'm going to load an example we prepared that mirrors a chat + summarization mix.
[02:00] Marcus Chen: (clicks) here is the request distribution slider, you can set the percent of traffic that's interactive versus batch. Riverbend, you mentioned 80% interactive during the daytime and a nightly 200k job?
[02:15] Daniel Ortiz: roughly yeah, 80/20 during peak days and nights the summarization spikes. the nightly job is large, memory heavy.
[02:26] Marcus Chen: okay so for the interactive 80% we show suggestions: a small prefix cache (per-conversation KV with LRU TTL 30m) plus conservative batching (target latency budget 250ms) — the model routing recommends smaller quantized backends for chat to meet latency. predicted token savings about 12-18% with no measurable tail latency increase in our sim.
[02:50] Priya Kumar: question — how do you measure the "predicted token savings"? is that based on real traces?
[02:57] Marcus Chen: good call, it's sample-based — the console takes a traffic trace you upload or sample stats you paste, runs a simulated run with heuristics for prefix hit rates, and then estimates reductions in total token generation and downstream rate-limited calls. it's not perfect but gives a directional delta.
[03:13] Evan Brooks: what about the summarization nightly job? sounds like batching should be full throughput there, any caching benefit?
[03:20] Ibrahim Patel: for large batch summarization, prefix cache is less useful unless you have repeated paragraphs across documents. more impact is in batching and model selection — e.g. quantized model variants or a lower-flops model for the heavy job. There we show a 28-35% cost reduction by switching model variant + aggressive batch size assuming memory fits.
[03:41] [03:45] Daniel Ortiz: memory fits is the kicker for us, our nightly job currently needs the high-memory instance. do you have a way to test that w/out us provisioning?
[03:53] Marcus Chen: yes, we can run a sandbox with your traces and virtualized memory constraints — that's one of the next steps. we'll do a simulated run that respects your peak mem numbers and give throughput/cost curves.
[04:05] Priya Kumar: cool. on the interactive side, our current redis hits are maybe 20% due to prompt variance. what prefetch heuristics do you recommend to improve that?
[04:15] Marcus Chen: two levers — lookahead prefetch based on user intent signals (clicks, previous messages) and prefix canonicalization (normalize prompts to improve hit rate). in the Console Optimize Playbook you can tune lookahead depth; we typically see an increase from 20% to 45-60% hits depending on prompt entropy.
[04:33] Lina Park: when you say 'prefetch depth' is that costed in the console? since extra prefetch means more tokens sometimes.
[04:39] Marcus Chen: yes we include prefetch delta in the costing model — we show incremental token rounds used for prefetch vs token savings on downstream generation. it's all in the Opportunity Map. often there's a sweet spot where limited prefetch yields net savings.
[04:52] [05:00] Sophie Lane: quick pause — wanted to highlight reliability controls: if prefetch fails or capacity is tight, the runtime will fall back to cold path and you can set throttles per-customer. that gives you guardrails so chat doesn't blow up if the cache layer is misbehaving.
[05:15] Daniel Ortiz: nice. we also have compliance: everything must stay in our VPC for production. how does Private deployment affect the Optimize recommendations?
[05:24] Ibrahim Patel: Optimize can run on Redwood Private; the console can operate via your private control plane. the cost model is identical but in Private you'll be looking at your infra costs rather than hosted unit prices — we can swap the unit economics in the model for a fair apples-to-apples.
[05:40] Priya Kumar: and KMS? we have strict key management, HSM.
[05:44] Marcus Chen: we integrate with KMS/HSM for Private. for hosted API we manage keys but we support customer-managed keys for some enterprise tiers. we'll add that to the security doc Sophie will share.
[05:55] [06:05] Marcus Chen: back to the UI, here's a scenario builder — i'm going to add two variants: conservative (prefetch depth 1, TTL 30m, batch window 20ms) and aggressive (prefetch depth 3, TTL 2h, batch window 60ms).
[06:25] Marcus Chen: now the Opportunity Map shows predicted monthly token delta, expected latency p95 change, and an error-rate proxy from routing to quantized models. conservative gives 10% token savings with p95 +10ms, aggressive gives 22% savings with p95 +40ms.
[06:42] Daniel Ortiz: god that's helpful. how confident are those error-rate numbers? our summaries must be within a certain quality threshold.
[06:50] Marcus Chen: we use a lightweight eval harness against a holdout prompt set you provide — it reports BLEU-style similarity and hallucination heuristics. quality regressions are flagged; you can configure hard gates so deployments revert if quality drops beyond X%.
[07:05] Priya Kumar: so you do automated rollback?
[07:08] Marcus Chen: yes, rollout policies include canary, A/B, and automatic fallback to a pinned model. that way you can test the aggressive profile on 5% of traffic first.
[07:17] [07:25] Evan Brooks: can the console recommendations export as Terraform or API calls? we try to keep infra as code.
[07:31] Ibrahim Patel: you can export runbooks and config JSON and we have APIs to create the routing policies; Terraform support is on the roadmap but we can provide a script for now.
[07:38] [08:00] Sophie Lane: Daniel, do you have the timelines / success criteria you mentioned earlier? what would success look like in 90 days?
[08:09] Daniel Ortiz: reduce interactive token spend by 15% without increasing p95 beyond 300ms and reduce nightly job cost by 25%, plus a safe pilot running in our VPC that doesn't touch prod data.
[08:23] Sophie Lane: perfect, that's clear. we'll map the Optimize scenarios to those goals and label them in the playbook.
[08:29] [08:40] Marcus Chen: okay i'll quickly show the trace upload flow — you can obfuscate PII, we accept gzipped JSON with timestamped requests and prompt/response token counts. once uploaded we run a 24-hour sim (fast path) and produce a savings matrix.
[09:00] Priya Kumar: do you need full user IDs? we avoid sharing them.
[09:03] Marcus Chen: no, anonymized session ids are fine. we just need relative sessionization signals and prompt lengths.
[09:10] Lina Park: a nit — will the console handle multi-model routing? we sometimes route to different families for different tenants.
[09:17] Ibrahim Patel: yes, multi-model routing is supported; you can define policies per-customer, per-route, and pen testers can pin variants.
[09:25] [09:40] Marcus Chen: showing the cost spreadsheet export now — this is the one Sophie will tailor. it has assumptions (token rates, request distribution, model variant costs). you can toggle hosted vs private pricing, and it recomputes net savings.
[10:00] Daniel Ortiz: what's the granularity of hosted unit pricing? is it per-token + per-request?
[10:05] Sophie Lane: hosted pricing combines a per-input-token and per-output-token rate plus an embedding request SKU; for Dedicated or Private we map to GPU-hour equivalent. the spreadsheet normalizes everything to a $/month baseline.
[10:20] Priya Kumar: on the technical side, any caveats about KV consistency? our Redis is strongly consistent and we worry about cache staleness on lookahead.
[10:28] Marcus Chen: good point — Redwood's KV layer for prefix cache is eventual by default for throughput; you can opt for strong consistency but that impacts latency. we usually recommend eventual with short TTLs for chat.
[10:40] Evan Brooks: can you TTL based on activity rather than absolute time? eg renew TTL on message?
[10:45] Ibrahim Patel: yes sliding TTLs are supported. that's often the best balance for active conversations.
[10:52] [11:10] Marcus Chen: let me show a micro-sim: taking a sample trace we imported from our test set, you can see per-route savings and a simulated p50/p95 latency chart with confidence bands.
[11:30] Marcus Chen: (shows chart) the shaded band shows uncertainty; for conservative strategy bars are narrow, aggressive wider. the Opportunity Map will attach recommended guardrails.
[11:45] Priya Kumar: and how do we operationalize alerts? we need to tie SLOs back to PagerDuty and our observability stack.
[11:52] Marcus Chen: Console has webhooks and integrations — we push trace-level anomalies and cost spikes. you can forward to your SIEM or set up PD rules from the webhooks.
[12:05] [12:30] Daniel Ortiz: earlier you mentioned model quantization tradeoffs for nightly jobs. can that be per-run? our job might need higher fidelity sometimes.
[12:38] Ibrahim Patel: yes the runbook can choose model variant per-run. you can schedule higher-fidelity runs for certain batches and fallback to quantized for the rest. the cost model will reflect mixed-run costs.
[12:52] Lina Park: curious about international/regulatory — will any metadata leave our region during the optimization sim?
[12:58] Sophie Lane: for Private we keep everything in your region. for hosted traces we scrub and the sim runs in the region selected. we'll note that in the security brief.
[13:10] [13:40] Marcus Chen: quick demo end — circling back to the 'opportunity map' pdf export: it lists per-route recommended profile, expected savings, latency delta, and the confidence level plus required changes (eg implement prefix canonicalization, add sliding TTL, set batch_window to 40ms).
[13:55] Daniel Ortiz: this was great — two follow-ups from us: Priya to give anonymized traces and Evan to share VPC constraints.
[14:03] Sophie Lane: noted — we'll send the tailored spreadsheet and run the sandbox sim. Marcus will own the sim.
[14:10] [14:30] Wrap and recap: Sophie Lane: recap: 1) Sophie to send cost spreadsheet + security docs by 2026-09-28 2) Marcus to run sandbox sim with Riverbend traces (target 2026-10-02) 3) follow-up 30m technical call to close on integration (week of 2026-10-05). any last q's?
[14:50] Priya Kumar: nothing else from me, thanks.
[14:52] Daniel Ortiz: no, thanks everyone.
[14:56] Sophie Lane: thanks all, we'll follow up in email.

End of recording.
